source.label: Opt-in logged-in browser social post ingestion
notes: Read-only browser automation through the user's authenticated OpenCLI browser session.
No likes, follows, comments, messages, saves, stars, subscriptions, profile edits, or other mutations are performed.
Instagram profile grids and X profile timelines are treated as opt-in authenticated/read-only sources when explicitly targeted.
X ingestion uses visible browser timeline parsing by default; high-level adapter fallback is disabled unless --allow-x-adapter-fallback is passed.
Logged-in LinkedIn activity scraping is disabled unless both --platforms=linkedin and --allow-linkedin are passed.
Each target is checkpointed independently; blocked or timed-out profiles are logged and do not stop the batch.

evidence.text: Inkbox (YC S26) is the identity and communication layer for AI agents: giving agents their own email, phone, iMessage, and internet address. Inkbox pulls together what your agent sees across email, calls, iMessage, and more, so your agent can act on the full context. Founders Ray Liao, Alex Wilcox, and Dima Vremenko came to the idea while building web-automation agents themselves. Every time an agent needed to log into a portal, it had to receive a confirmation email or a 2FA code. Contacting the agents on the go meant stitching together Gmail, Twilio, ngrok, and more: separate services, each built for humans, none sharing identity or context. So they built the thing they wished existed. With one Inkbox API, every agent gets a unique email inbox (with custom domain), a phone number that can call and text, iMessage, a persistent HTTPS address for webhooks, and an encrypted credential vaul

evidence.text: Trope (YC S26) is the AI-native platform built for ERP implementations. Buying an ERP is easy. Implementation is where it breaks. Consultants juggle hundreds of stakeholders, thousands of documents, and endless configuration decisions that determine the business processes of a company. Trope understands ERP implementations across calls, docs, and the ERP itself. Trope deploys agents to take action - it’s like a project manager, consultant, and developer working 24/7, so implementation teams can focus on the people and processes. evidence.text: After leaving Georgia Tech in January to build a startup full-time, I'm beyond excited to share that 6thSense is now backed by Y Combinator! Founding a deeptech company has been a longtime dream, and I couldn't be happier doing it with my best friends Hyungwoo Noh, Ronak Agarwal, and Matt Wulff. Robots still can't feel the world, and the data to teach them doesn't exist. So we built a wearable that captures exactly that. Every frame records what the hands see and feel: pressure across every finger, object contact, and 3D hand pose — in any kitchen, any hallway, anywhere. Not a lab. The real world. We believe this is the missing layer for teaching robots dexterity and mastering manipulation. So, if you're building robots or training manipulation models and want richer tactile + vision data, let's talk — we're working with a handful of teams now. Always happy to connect with others pushing

evidence.text: Most dealerships are losing $10K per customer... Not because they're bad at selling cars. Because they're too focused on selling cars. Here's what I mean: The average front-end gross on a car deal? Maybe $500. The lifetime value of that same customer through service and F&I? $8,000–$12,000. Yet most dealers will spend hours grinding over the sale… then never follow up after the customer drives off the lot. It's like Gillette selling you the razor handle for $5 — and then making $200/year on blades for the next decade. The car isn't the product. It's the razor. Squeezed in a selfie with Garry Tan, Paul Graham, and Jessica Livingston at YC! 📸😁

Growing up, I used to read Paul Graham’s essays like they were scripture.

I watched every YC talk on YouTube. Read everything I could find about how he and Jessica built it from nothing. Two people who just believed the best founders were out there, overlooked, underestimated, and decided to bet on them anyway.

They shaped how I think. How I build. How I see the world.

This week, they came to YC to give a talk.

And I was sitting in the room.

After years of reading the words on a screen, I got to hear it in person. The early days. The doubt. The sheer amount of hardwork behind everything that looks inevitable in hindsight.

It reminded me that nothing starts polished. Everything great starts somewhere small and uncertain and a little scary.

We are 8 days from Demo Day. @saudara.ai let's goo! 🚀

Somewhere became here.

evidence.text: I’m happy to share that I’m founding 83 Sciences (YC S26) where we are building the “lab brain” for academic labs. We're working with our first cohort of labs now, together with my cofounders Eric Riesel and Yankang Yang. evidence.rawVisibleText: Feed post number 5 Warren Shepard reposted this Jack Grodnick Jack Grodnick • 3rd+ Verified • 3rd+ Co-Founder @ Control Seat (YC S26) Co-Founder @ Control Seat (YC S26) 3w • Edited • 3 weeks ago • Edited • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn Follow Excited to announce that Warren Shepard and I were accepted into the Y Combinator Summer 2026 batch 🥳 The lead-up to this has been anything but smooth. College has been the toughest time of my life. Last year, I took leave from school after losing my younger brother, among many other things. Somehow, during that time, I still managed to interview for some of my dream roles at companies I’ve admired for years. Originally, I was planning on spending my gap year at SpaceX, but right before I signed my internship extension, I sat down with my mentor and told him I’d be heading back to my mom’s basement to start a company. I’m pretty sure he thought I was a little crazy. A week later, Warren and I got the call that we’d been accepted into YC. I rejected all my return offers and went all in. I’ve always loved building. I love making things better and trying to build the world I envisioned as a kid. It’s what I've tried my best to mirror in my professional life. I thought working on Starship would satisfy that, but I realized I’d be spending more time fighting the systems I was using than helping get humanity to Mars. That’s when I realized the problems I was most passionate about solving were the ones slowing down the people trying to build the future. That's why Warren and I started Control Seat (YC S26). We're building a data analytics platform for industrial operations because the people running factories, power systems, and critical infrastructure deserve better tools. Long term, our goal is to bring control, monitoring, and analytics into a single platform. I just wanted to thank everyone who has supported me and taken a chance on me: my Tesla/Amazon friends and mentors for opening my eyes to the world and the incredible learning experiences that set me up to do this, my SpaceX team (who I have no doubt will get humanity to Mars), and all of my friends at Dartmouth College who supported me through some difficult times. And most importantly, my mom and family for supporting me to get here. evidence.text: 100s of people ask me what Y Combinator is like and what we're building with LATO (YC S26). Here's a raw look at both - fun meta moment at 35 sec! LATO helps investors understand companies and markets. One of the best ways to do that is to talk to the people who know or use them - domain experts. That's what we're building LATO to do - at a speed and depth that wasn't possible before. In the short video I show 2 things: 1) creating a study live on how YC founders use agents, with the voice agent interviewing me 2) results from a study on how recruiters use AI, where LATO automatically found the right domain experts, interviewed them, and surfaced the key themes If you want to understand companies and markets faster and go deeper, reach out. Visit my website 1w • 1 week ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn Follow We are excited to announce that we got into YC S26! 🔥 Same team, sharper idea. HyperTest has now become HyperProbe. Our mission is to enable coding agents to remotely debug running systems, and here's why it's crucial now. AI is now responsible for writing most of our code, yet observability still operates under the assumption that a human wrote it. Humans traditionally add logs to lines and decide in advance what is worth logging based on their intuition about what might matter. This entire model relies on the author having an understanding of where the code might be fragile. However, the AI-coding explosion challenges this paradigm. Agents lack that instinct. When an agent writes code, there is no mental model formed about where it might break, meaning the log line needed when it fails is often missing. As agents write more code, the amount of code that ships without useful instrumentation in critical areas continues to grow. Additionally, the context required for debugging keeps diminishing. We are building HyperProbe to invert this dependency. Instead of pre-instrumenting code, agents can insert non-blocking probes into the running system after identifying what they are looking for. Scoped to the exact issue, requiring no redeploy and eliminating guesswork. Debug the code your agents wrote with evidence rather than inference. More updates coming soon. evidence.title: Alex Hyungwoo Noh LinkedIn post
evidence.text: Robots are getting great at seeing the world. They're still terrible at touching it. The reason is data. There's an ocean of video to learn from, and almost nothing that captures what a hand actually feels - the pressure, the contact, the grip - while doing real tasks in real homes. At 6thSense, we built a wearable that captures exactly that. Every frame records what the hands see and feel: pressure across every finger, object contact, and 3D hand pose - in any kitchen, any hallway, anywhere. Not a lab. The real world. We believe this is the missing layer for teaching robots dexterity and master manipulation tasks. evidence.rawVisibleText: Feed post number 4 Sanjukta B. reposted this Atlas Discovery Atlas Discovery 191 followers 191 followers 2w • 2 weeks ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn Follow Nine out of ten drugs fail in clinical trials. Most failures happen because nothing in the lab reliably predicts how a person will respond, and the data that could close that gap sits in silos that rarely connect a patient's biology to whether the drug worked. At Atlas Discovery, we're building foundation models of patient drug response. We learn the structure of human biology once, across millions of pre-clinical and clinical samples, so a single trial only has to learn the last step: who responds and who doesn't. We've tested this across a number of clinical studies and seen strong results. From a single biopsy taken before treatment, our model predicts which ulcerative colitis patients would respond to ustekinumab at 0.76 AUROC. Applied to the UNIFI phase 3 trial, that accuracy would have reached the same statistical power with 458 fewer patients, 182 instead of 640. The trial has always been our coarsest model of the patient, averaging over everyone because we couldn't predict any one person. As prediction improves, more of the evidence shifts into the model, where it's faster, cheaper, and specific to an individual. That means trials designed to succeed, drugs written off too early getting a second look, and treatments that were never practical to test becoming feasible to run. We're backed by investors including Y Combinator, Pear VC, and Glasswing Ventures. evidence.text: 📣 My first first-author paper is officially published! As many people with arthritis know, human joints don’t grow back once they’re damaged. To better understand how we might one day change that, we developed a new model for joint regeneration using zebrafish – an animal that can regenerate its joints. 🐟 In our study, we created a new way to study joint regeneration by removing the entire jaw joint in adult zebrafish. We discovered that they are able to fully regrow a functional joint, complete with lubricating articular cartilage. At the Smeeton Lab, our goal is to use this zebrafish model to discover cellular and genetic targets for improving the regenerative abilities of human joints. evidence.title: Daniela Muñoz LinkedIn post
evidence.text: I have never been this excited about anything. Last year, it took me using OpenClaw for all of 5 minutes to realize that the world is fundamentally changing. Technology is moving fast enough to completely rewrite how people work, what a small team can pull off, and who gets to build at all. And it’s only accelerating. I immediately turned to Jordan and I told him I want to be a part of this. It was simply too exciting not to. We dropped everything. We started talking to everyone we knew about how they were using AI. What did they know? What did they wish they could do? What was holding them back? A pattern showed up immediately. The people building and using these tools live in a bubble. evidence.rawVisibleText: Feed post number 5 Sanjukta B. reposted this Shaamil Karim Shaamil Karim • 3rd+ Premium • 3rd+ CEO @ Atlas Discovery | YC S26 CEO @ Atlas Discovery | YC S26 2mo • Edited • 2 months ago • Edited • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn Follow Excited to present our virtual cell paper at the ICLR conference in Rio this week. Virtual cells are AI models that can predict how cells respond to perturbations like drugs or gene knockouts. Getting this right could mean screening drugs and disease targets using virtual cells before committing billions of dollars and years on clinical trials. We introduced a virtual cell model that uses a discrete diffusion framework to operate directly on raw gene expression counts. Diffusion is a popular framework these days for language modeling; turns out you can use the underlying machinery for virtual cell gene expression modelling as well. This improves unconditional cell-type generation by 5x. When the model is given immune cells and asked how it responds to a cytokine treatment, we find over 2x improvement in matching ground-truth gene expression. Prior virtual cell models (scGPT, STATE, scLDM) takes discrete integer counts of gene expression, relaxes them into continuous vectors, and recovers discreteness only at the output. This hurts the representational power of the model. We're also excited about the possibilities that using a discrete modelling technique opens up, like interpretability and sample efficiency in gene expression learning. These promising results are from our model with 10 million parameters. Language models today have trillions. We've barely started scaling virtual cells, and the frontiers of innovation will be data, modeling, and benchmarks. We'll share our work on all three soon. Thank you to my collaborators, Sanjukta B. and Christian G., for their work. We’re grateful for the folks at Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, Arc Institute, and everyone pushing virtual cells forward. Our model weights are open-source in our preprint linked below. We’ll be presenting at the MLGenX workshop. evidence.text: What does real-world decarbonization look like? Harvard Business School students share insights from their deep dive into decarbonization within the steel industry, culminating in an impactful visit to JSW Steel's Dolvi plant. From case discussions on campus to witnessing their ambitious net-zero 2050 targets firsthand, students explored the challenges and opportunities of balancing growth with sustainability. Students were impressed by JSW's "Project SEED," empowering every employee to contribute to emission reduction and, while their commitment to innovation and safety was evident, the visit underscored the critical need for policy interventions to drive meaningful decarbonization in the face of rising steel demand. evidence.title: Parth Ajmera LinkedIn post
evidence.text: Just read an interesting blog. DeepSeek's DSpark makes V4 up to 85% faster per user. No retraining. No new hardware. No quality loss. Same exact output, just sooner. The base idea is speculative decoding: a small, fast model guesses the next few tokens, and the big model verifies the whole guess in a single pass instead of writing word by word. The math keeps it lossless. What makes DSpark clever is the reframe. It stops asking "how do we guess more?" and starts asking "what's even worth checking?" Two moves: 1. Give the fast guesser a tiny memory, so it stops producing "of problem" instead of "of course." 2. Predict which guesses will survive, and check more when the GPU is idle, fewer when it's slammed. The part worth sitting with: a. This is a systems win, not a smarter model. The weights never changed. b. And because it's lossless, your evals won't move at all. The speedup only shows

evidence.text: The Black Box problem is officially moving from the R&D lab to the Boardroom. evidence.title: Mohit Gupta LinkedIn post
evidence.text: credit fund completely alone. No analysts. No ops team. No CFO. One person. I assumed I misheard him. I've watched 20-person teams manage the same AUM and still drown in spreadsheets. He described his fund as "one giant algorithm": Collateral pool → trust → waterfall → hedge → fund → LP reporting → management company budget. All reports get ingested and reconciled automatically. The part that surprised me most: he barely uses LLMs at runtime. AI writes his apps. The apps themselves are deterministic. Data in, data out. He won't let a model interpret anything that touches money. "I don't want the LLM making decisions for me." Decisions stay human. Everything else is code. Then he said the thing I keep replaying: "The funds running 20 people on $200M need to fire 15 of them. Because I'll do it cheaper. Fees are coming down massively." Every fund he competes against is carrying 15 salaries

evidence.text: The workshops explained what AI can do. The hallways were about the bill. Last week I was at a developer summit in Bangalore. Every track was about AI-first workflows — coding, debugging, incident response. Good content, full rooms. But outside these sessions, developers actively building these workflows had completely different learnings to share [.] Tools have become more agentic -> consume more compute [.] Consumption pattern of devs 10-100x a casual user -> Claude Max tier ($200/month) is maxxing out in 20 minutes of active coding [.] Costs are predictable for light users -> more variable for power users [.] Flat seat pricing going away -> actual token usage replacing request quotas My takeaway from the conference was two critical concerns dev wanted to plan their AI usage going forward [1] Token consumption will be a first-class engineering concern Coding is the worst case for token
evidence.rawVisibleText: Feed post number 5 Shailendra Singh Shailendra Singh • 3rd+ Verified • 3rd+ Founder, HyperProbe 🚀 | YC S26 | Debug production live | AI finds root cause, places breakpoints, captures state. Fix incidents in minutes, not hours. Founder, HyperProbe 🚀 | YC S26 | Debug production live | AI finds root cause, places breakpoints, captures state. Fix incidents in minutes, not hours. Visit my website 2mo • 2 months ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn Follow The workshops explained what AI can do. The hallways were about the bill. Last week I was at a developer summit in Bangalore. Every track was about AI-first workflows — coding, debugging, incident response. Good content, full rooms. But outside these sessions, developers actively building these workflows had completely different learnings to share [.] Tools have become more agentic -> consume more compute [.] Consumption pattern of devs 10-100x a casual user -> Claude Max tier ($200/month) is maxxing out in 20 minutes of active coding [.] Costs are predictable for light users -> more variable for power users [.] Flat seat pricing going away -> actual token usage replacing request quotas My takeaway from the conference was two critical concerns dev wanted to plan their AI usage going forward [1] Token consumption will be a first-class engineering concern Coding is the worst case for token economics. The closer next is RCA using logs. Logs are verbose, written for humans and expensive to reason, hence low signal <-> high noise is becoming norm. Unlike experimental AI usage, these costs will scale with engineering activity. Frontier capability will get increasingly expensive, and teams will be forced to architect for tasks which actually need the frontier models. [2] Model performance has stopped improving but costs continue to increase Specific to frontier reasoning models doing agentic tasks . Anthropic tightened peak-hour session limits, Opus 4.6 became less capable for more complex tasks; performance regression everybody have felt Anthropic also shipped a new tokenizer with 'adaptive' that consumes 1 to 1.35x more tokens per unit of text. The control of setting thinking tokens taken away. So predictability is gone, not just price Maybe next year the same crowd come back to check if others learnt to use AI within budget. So would teams consider moving to cheaper models for costs or continue working with expensive reasoning models for performance? hashtag #devsummit hashtag #engineering P.S. We are building a way to help coding agents debug a production incidents faster but burning 1/10th tokens. Not with logs, but snapshots. evidence.rawVisibleText: Feed post number 2 Sanjukta B. Sanjukta B. • 3rd+ Premium • 3rd+ Co Founder @ Atlas Discovery (YC S26) Co Founder @ Atlas Discovery (YC S26) 1w • Edited • 1 week ago • Edited • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn Follow We embedded baseline colon biopsies from the UNIFI phase 3 trial (ustekinumab in ulcerative colitis) using a foundational model of patient biology, trained a small supervised head on top, and predicted week-8 clinical response at AUROC 0.76 from a 358-patient cohort. We also derive an interpretation of the model weights for this. Why that number matters more than it looks: single-analytic companion diagnostics in immunology and oncology have lived at 0.55–0.65 for years not because the biology is missing, but because you can't fit a 20k-dimensional response rule on a few hundred patients. The trick isn't a better trial-specific model. It's moving the hard part out of the trial entirely. Pretrain once across millions of samples so the biological state lives in a geometry where responders cluster; then the trial only has to learn which directions in that latent space separate responders from non-responders. We also ran a linear probe across the learned features, and the top 30 genes show coherent themes: MMP7, CHI3L1, IL6, CXCL10, CXCL13, and CD38 are linked with mucosal inflammation in IBD, while IDO1, COL23A1, and MS4A7 mark the non-responder phenotype of chronic, less immunologically active. It seems the consequence is structural here. We worked out a closed form for trial size as a function of biomarker AUROC, and in the operational range each 0.01 of AUROC buys ~5% fewer patients (roughly linear, no diminishing returns until you hit the prevalence floor - we show how in our blog). Applied retrospectively to UNIFI: ~91 patients/arm instead of 320 at matched power. Two things I want to clarify: 1. You can't actually enrich a trial with a model trained on that same trial, this is a retrospective demonstration of the relationship between AUROC, power, and N, not a claim UNIFI was oversized. 2. Power isn't the only thing that sets trial size. Safety exposure floors and regulatory patient-years impose their own minima that biomarker enrichment can't collapse. What it changed for me is smaller and more personal: it's the first real evidence that the thing I've been staring at loss curves for is learning the structure of human disease, not just memorizing it. The trial has always been our coarsest model of a patient: treatment, disease, stage, average over everything else. Every gain in individual response prediction relocates a little evidence out of the trial (slow, expensive, aggregate) and into the model (fast, cheap, specific to a person). One drug, one indication, one cohort, a model trained on a fraction of the data that exists. I'd read the result as a lower bound. A lot of progress to be made, at Atlas Discovery with Christian G. and Shaamil Karim ! Full writeup in the comments. Would love thoughts, and feedback on this result, our approach from anyone working on trial design, and AI for biology research. …more 9 2 comments 2 reposts Like Comment Repost Send

evidence.title: Eric Taylor LinkedIn post
evidence.text: Companies are increasingly leveraging LLMs for coding tasks such as code generation, documentation, and test creation. With thousands of runs per day, costs can quickly add up, whether using APIs, cloud solutions, or in-house machines. A key question arises: What size LLM is needed for a given task? Do complex tests require an 8 billion-parameter model, or can a 1.5 billion-parameter model suffice? Understanding this tradeoff is essential, as larger models can be significantly more expensive at scale. My Software Verification project with Hengchen Yuan and Arsh Guntakal explores an adaptive approach to optimize costs by selecting smaller models for simpler code and reserving larger models for complex cases. Specifically, we use static code metrics to assess how well different model sizes perform in generating test suites for specific code blocks. -ET …more

evidence.title: Jonathan Waldorf LinkedIn post
evidence.text: It's context. Our bottleneck is always context. Our CTO’s Claude didn't know what our COO’s Codex was doing. Every few hours, it felt like half our prompts became asking Fable to read .mds and update them if necessary. All before running meetings, to make sure we – the human devs – were also all on the same page. It was incredibly wasteful. So we built Compendium. A shared workspace where every teammate and every AI agent works from the same synchronized context. evidence.title: Shailendra Singh LinkedIn post
evidence.text: The most expensive bugs in production don't throw exceptions. Not the ones that crash. The ones that succeed with wrong outputs. Here's a failure mode I keep seeing in fleet and logistics apps. ⚠️ A truck location update doesn't reach the customer dashboard ⚠️ A user-specific notification fails to fire ⚠️ Pricing calculation returns number within valid range, just wrong for that user The code ran. The API returned 200. No 500 error. No stack trace. No PagerDuty alert. The first signal is a customer escalation, days later. evidence.rawVisibleText: Feed post number 3 Shailendra Singh Shailendra Singh • 3rd+ Verified • 3rd+ Founder, HyperProbe 🚀 | YC S26 | Debug production live | AI finds root cause, places breakpoints, captures state. Fix incidents in minutes, not hours. Founder, HyperProbe 🚀 | YC S26 | Debug production live | AI finds root cause, places breakpoints, captures state. Fix incidents in minutes, not hours. Visit my website 1mo • 1 month ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn Follow The most expensive bugs in production don't throw exceptions. Not the ones that crash. The ones that succeed with wrong outputs. Here's a failure mode I keep seeing in fleet and logistics apps. ⚠️ A truck location update doesn't reach the customer dashboard ⚠️ A user-specific notification fails to fire ⚠️ Pricing calculation returns number within valid range, just wrong for that user The code ran. The API returned 200. No 500 error. No stack trace. No PagerDuty alert. The first signal is a customer escalation, days later. I've spent the last few months talking to engineering leaders at fleet, logistics, and operations-heavy companies. Teams spend hours debugging issues that their alert system never caught. Why. → No exception means no stack trace. we are working backwards from a vague user complaint, not a failure point. → The flow that broke is one of thousands running per minute. Can't add logs to every line and redeploy hoping to catch it. → By the time the customer escalates, the specific user, the specific request, the specific state has all been overwritten a million times. Our logs, traces, error trackers, answers what our code told us it is doing. None of them tell us what our code is doing for the user who complained. The ticket gets closed as not reproducible. That is the gap. We're building HyperProbe to fix exactly this. Engineer opens VS Code, right-clicks on the function they suspect, drop a non-breaking breakpoint scoped to a specific user or condition. Service keeps running, no redeploy. The next time that flow executes for user, capture complete application state, variable values, watch expressions, call stack, DB state, at that exact line. The bug doesn't have to fail. It just has to run. Our APM tells us which APIs threw errors. evidence.title: Saksham Gupta LinkedIn post
evidence.text: credit fund completely alone. No analysts. No ops team. No CFO. One person. I assumed I misheard him. I've watched 20-person teams manage the same AUM and still drown in spreadsheets. He described his fund as "one giant algorithm": Collateral pool → trust → waterfall → hedge → fund → LP reporting → management company budget. All reports get ingested and reconciled automatically. The part that surprised me most: he barely uses LLMs at runtime. AI writes his apps. The apps themselves are deterministic. Data in, data out. He won't let a model interpret anything that touches money. "I don't want the LLM making decisions for me." Decisions stay human. Everything else is code. Then he said the thing I keep replaying: "The funds running 20 people on $200M need to fire 15 of them. Because I'll do it cheaper. Fees are coming down massively." Every fund he competes against is carrying 15 salaries

We analysed 15,000 founders using five binary signals to measure this: odd hobbies, early signs of exceptionalism, extreme life choices, unusual geographies, non-linear careers. These sum to give a 0-5 score per founder. Whether someone started coding at 10, speaks five languages, climbed Everest or quit a safe job to live in Chile, the signal was deviation from the mean.

Rather than focusing on IQ or EQ, we call this metric the Outlier Quotient, or “OQ”. When forecasting founder success, it turns out that OQ was the single most predictive variable in our entire classification model, trained on ~70 different factors.

Our OQ score had zero correlation with having worked at a top-tier company or attending an elite university. The signals most VCs rely on aren’t just noisy, they’re blinding. The best founders don’t signal like everyone else, they don’t think like everyone else, and they certainly don’t build like everyone else. 

If you want to spot breakout talent before the rest of the market, stop screening for conformity. evidence.text: A few years ago, Anchit Kumar and I were standing in the Mojave Desert trying to hot fire a cryogenic rocket engine. We knew the engine would be hard. That was the part everyone warned us about. What we didn’t expect was how much time we’d lose to everything around the test. Getting sensors online. Checking configs. Updating procedures. Watching redlines. Digging through logs late at night trying to figure out what changed since the last run. evidence.text: We asked whether we could predict which patients respond to a drug from a single biopsy, taken before treatment. Using a foundation model of patient biology, we predicted response to ustekinumab in IBD at 0.76 AUROC, from baseline biopsies alone. Applied to UNIFI, the phase 3 trial it was trained on, that is the difference between 320 patients per arm and 91, at the same statistical power. Roughly 450 fewer patients for the same answer. Then we opened the box to do some interpretability. Using SHAP and Lasso probes we traced the prediction back to specific genes. The signal lines up with biology IBD researchers already know: MMP7, CHI3L1, IL6, CXCL10/13, CD38 for inflammation; IDO1 and fibrosis markers for non-response. Our interpretability was validated by IBD experts and our pharma collaborators. Pathway enrichment tells the same story: interferon response, TNF-α/NF-κB signaling, chemo

evidence.text: It breaks my heart every time I hear about someone losing a loved one to a disease like cancer or alzheimer’s. Christian, Sanjukta, and I started Atlas Discovery to help get treatments to the patients who need them most. The biology that drives response in a real human is hard to see from preclinical work alone. This is largely why nine out of ten drugs fail in clinical trials. We train foundation models on both preclinical and clinical data to predict patient response to drugs. We've tested this across a number of clinical studies and seen strong results. On a phase 3 IBD trial (UNIFI), our model correctly distinguishes responders from non-responders 76% of the time. Our goal is to use these models to improve clinical trial success
